g.text: One path needs a distributed claim. The other structurally cannot race - and saying which is which is the point.
Matchmaking runs on many instances claiming the same pair of players. A game's moves run on exactly one instance, by construction.
Two explicit state machines, both with one-way terminal transitions
active
completed checkmate | resignation | draw | timeout
abandoned
GameStatus - both terminal, one-way,
and mutually exclusive
queued
widening
matched
cancelled
MatchmakingTicket
Modelling both as named enums with enforced transitions - not a free-text status or a pair
of booleans - is what makes 'A FINISHED GAME NEVER RE-SCORES' and 'A MATCHED TICKET IS
NEVER RE-MATCHED' checkable at the type level rather than by review.
MatchmakingPool -> RatingBucketedPool
enqueue(player_id, rating, time_control)
findCandidates(player_id, rating, window)
removeBoth(player_id_a, player_id_b) # the ATOMIC claim
ChessEngine -> StandardChessRules
isLegalMove / applyMove / isCheckmate / isDraw
MoveLogWriter -> AppendOnlyMoveLog
append(game_id, move, ply, ts) / replay(game_id)
RatingService -> EloRatingService
expectedScore(a, b) / update(a, b, result, k)
SessionRouter -> ConsistentHashSessionRouter
assign(game_id) / locate(game_id)
GameSession the per-game orchestrator, owning board_state
Every legality decision in the entire system goes through ONE interface, so a variant
ruleset like Chess960 is a second implementation behind it - never a rewrite of
GameSession. And MoveLogWriter.replay is used ONLY by the crash-recovery and
reconnection paths, never by the hot move-validation path.
Matchmaking: a widening window, oldest ticket first
MatchFormationService.tick():
for ticket in pool.allWaitingSortedByWaitTime(): # oldest first - FAIRNESS
window = widen(ticket.wait_seconds)
for candidate in pool.findCandidates(ticket.player_id,
ticket.rating, window):
if candidate.player_id == ticket.player_id: continue
if pool.removeBoth(ticket.player_id,
candidate.player_id): # ATOMIC CONDITIONAL
game_id = allocateGame(ticket, candidate)
instance = sessionRouter.assign(game_id)
notify(both players, game_id, instance)
break # this ticket is resolved - on to the next
widen(wait_seconds) -> rating points
A wider window trades match quality for wait time -
and the trade only ever moves in one direction, which
is what keeps it predictable.
pool.removeBoth() is the ENTIRE concurrency-safety mechanism for matchmaking, deliberately mirroring the job scheduler's atomic
claim: many MatchFormationService instances run this tick concurrently, and for a given pair of players only ONE instance's
removeBoth call can succeed.
Live move validation - and why the turn check comes before the legality check
GameSession.onMove(player_id, client_seq, from, to, promotion):
if client_seq <= lastAppliedSeq[player_id]:
return currentState() # retried/duplicate - safe NO-OP
if player_id != board_state.turn_player:
raise IllegalMove('not your turn')
if not chessEngine.isLegalMove(board_state, from, to, promotion):
raise IllegalMove('illegal move')
board_state = chessEngine.applyMove(board_state, move)
lastAppliedSeq[player_id] = client_seq
moveLogWriter.append(game_id, move, ply, now()) # async
broadcastToBothPlayers('move.applied', board_state, move)
if chessEngine.isCheckmate(board_state) or isDraw(board_state):
endGame(result=...) # -> RatingService.update(...)
return board_state
The turn_player check happening BEFORE legality, not after, is deliberate: an
out-of-turn move should never even reach the more expensive legal-move check. The
cheapest, most decisive rejection reason comes first.
And the client_seq guard makes a retried submit a safe no-op rather than a second
move - the same idempotency-key shape as everywhere else in this guide, at
per-connection scope rather than per-payment.
GameSession.onMove is the DELIBERATE EXCEPTION to 'push atomicity down into the
store'. Because the Session Router pins BOTH players' connections for a given
game_id to exactly one instance, there is no second instance that could ever race
this method for the same game. A lightweight in-process guard - or simply
processing each game's moves single-threaded, actor-style - is correct and
sufficient. Reaching for a distributed claim here would be solving a race that
structurally cannot happen on this path.
By contrast, removeBoth needs one precisely BECAUSE a language-level mutex would
only protect threads on the same instance, and do nothing about a peer instance
claiming the same pair a moment later.
The rating update, concretely - and why both players update in one call
E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B - R_A) / 400)) # a SMOOTH function of the gap
S_A = 1 (win) | 0.5 (draw) | 0 (loss)
R_A' = R_A + K * (S_A - E_A)
The K-FACTOR controls how much a single game can move a rating: a new, provisional
player uses a LARGER K, because their early games should correct a bad initial
estimate fast; an established player uses a smaller one, because a single upset
should not swing a stable rating wildly.
Both ratings update from the same game in ONE call, because E_A + E_B = 1 and the
two deltas are equal and opposite - the same reasoning a double-entry ledger uses
for a debit and a credit always summing to zero, applied to a rating exchange
instead of money.
Four error cases designed for deliberately
a move arrives for a game_id this instance does not hold
a stale client routing entry, or a reconnect that raced the Session Router. Rejected outright, with the client redirected via
sessionRouter.locate(game_id) - rather than the instance guessing at intent.
an illegal or out-of-turn move
rejected with a SPECIFIC reason, never silently dropped and never 'corrected' on the client's behalf. The client finds out
exactly why - which is what the never-trust-the-client requirement actually demands.
a disconnect mid-game
NOT an immediate forfeit. GameSession starts a bounded abandonment timer (60 s, longer for a slower time control), and
reconnection inside that window resumes from board_state exactly as it stood - with no special-cased 'recovering a dropped
game' logic beyond the normal reconnection path.
the Game Server instance itself restarts mid-game
board_state is not held anywhere durable BY DESIGN - it is the fast path, not the source of truth. A restarting instance calls
moveLogWriter.replay(game_id) and rebuilds board_state by re-applying every persisted move in order: the same event-log-replay
shape the real-time leaderboard uses to rebuild its sorted set after a crash.
Patterns, named - including the one that is genuinely different from this guide's default
Repository MatchmakingPool and MoveLogWriter hide storage behind method calls; neither MatchFormationService nor
GameSession issues a raw query or cache command directly
Strategy ChessEngine (standard rules versus a variant) and RatingService (Elo versus another system), both
swappable behind one interface with no caller knowing which is active
State, via an enum GameStatus and MatchmakingTicket's enforced one-way transitions - the same discipline as PaymentStatus
and DeliveryStatus elsewhere in this guide
ACTOR-PER-GAME worth naming explicitly, because it is the one pattern here that differs from this guide's
stateless-request-handler default: GameSession is a SINGLE-WRITER, SINGLE-INSTANCE owner of one game's
state for that game's entire life - which is exactly what makes the concurrency reasoning above hold.
